paragraphs: Family-owned businesses often outlast their rivals through downturns, a resilience commonly credited to owners' willingness to forgo dividends and accept lower pay when times are hard. The same attachment can become a liability when leadership passes to the next generation. Founders who built the firm from nothing tend to value it for what it produces; heirs, who inherited it, may value it chiefly as a family possession to be preserved, and a business run to preserve rather than to grow tends to stagnate. Studies that compare firms led by heirs with those led by outside managers hired by the family generally find that outsiders deliver faster growth. Yet this comparison is imperfect, because families that hire outsiders may do so only when the firm is already healthy enough to attract capable candidates. The sensible conclusion is not that heirs should be excluded but that the family should ask, at each handover, which kind of leader the firm now needs.
